{{short description|German-Hungarian astronomer (1756–1828)}}

'''David ben Meir Cohen Friesenhausen''' (1756–1828) was a German-Hungarian astronomer, ''[[maskil]]'', mathematician, and rabbi.<ref name="YIVO">{{cite web|url=http://www.yivoencyclopedia.org/article.aspx/Friesenhausen_David|title=Friesenhausen, David|last=Silber|first=Michael K.|publisher=[[YIVO]]|accessdate=9 August 2014}}</ref><ref name="JE1906" /> Friesenhausen was one of the first proponents of ''[[Torah im Derech Eretz]]'',<ref name="BROWN" /><ref name="LEIMAN">{{cite book|last=Leiman|first=Shanyor Z. |editor=Jacob J. Schacter|title=Judaism's Encounter with Other Cultures: Rejection or Integration?|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=l2PfY74QF7IC&pg=PA158|year=1997|publisher=[[Jason Aronson]]|isbn=1-4616-2928-4|pages=158–159}}</ref> a philosophy of [[Orthodox Judaism]] that formalizes a relationship between traditionally observant Judaism and the modern world.<ref name="EISENBERG">{{cite book|last=Ronald L. Eisenberg|first=Ronald L. Eisenberg|title=Essential Figures in Jewish Scholarship|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=osM0AwAAQBAJ&pg=PA248|year=2014|publisher=[[Rowman & Littlefield]]|isbn=978-0-7657-0995-0|page=248}}</ref> He proposed a dual curriculum of Jewish and secular studies for all rabbinic candidates,<ref name="BROWN" /> a radically innovative idea at that time.<ref name="Patai" /> Friesenhausen wrote ''Mosedot Tebel'' and ''Kelil Heshbon''. In the former, Friesenhausen writes in support of the [[Copernican heliocentrism]], one of the first Jews to do so.<ref name="LEIMAN" />

== Early life ==
In 1756, David Friesenhausen was born in [[Friesenhausen]], a small community in southern Germany, {{convert|60|mi|km|sigfig=1|order=flip}} northeast of Frankfurt.<ref name="BROWN">{{cite book|last=Brown|first=Jeremy|title=New Heavens and a New Earth: The Jewish Reception of Copernican Thought|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YQ1J-W6kuSkC&pg=168|date=14 June 2013|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|isbn=978-0-19-975479-3|pages=168–170}}</ref>  In 1783, Friesenhausen married, but was divorced four years later.<ref name="BROWN" /> For the first 30 years of his life, Friesenhausen dedicated himself exclusively [[Torah]] study.<ref name="YIVO" /> His teachers included [[Joseph Steinhardt]] at Fürth and [[Moses Sofer]] of Pressburg.<ref name="YIVO" /> The latter attested that Friesenhausen was one of the outstanding students in his yeshiva.<ref name="YIVO" />  In 1786, Friesenhausen began immersing himself in various secular subjects, including math, astronomy, and philosophy.<ref name="YIVO" /><ref name="LEIMAN" />

== Berlin ==
In 1788, Friesenhausen moved to Berlin where he lived for the next eight years and was supported by Benjamin Halberstat.<ref name="BROWN" /> Berlin at that time was the center of the ''[[haskala]]'' movement (Jewish Enlightenment).<ref name="LEIMAN" /> Despite his involvement in secular subjects, Friesenhausen continued to study Torah intensively.<ref name="LEIMAN" />  In 1796, Friesenhausen published his first book, ''Kelil Heshbon'' a Hebrew language manual on algebra and trigonometry.<ref name="JE1906" /><ref name="BROWN" /><ref name="Patai">{{cite book|last=Patai|first=Raphael|authorlink=Raphael Patai|title=The Jews of Hungary: History, Culture, Psychology|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LLuPS1yVDf8C&pg=PA242|year=1996|publisher=[[Wayne State University Press]]|isbn=0-8143-2561-0|pages=242–244}}</ref> Thereafter, Friesenhausen left Berlin to travel throughout Europe for the dual purpose of selling  his newly published book and to attain advance subscriptions for planned book, ''Mosodot Tevel''.<ref name="Patai" />

== Huncovce ==
Around 1800, Friesenhausen moved to [[Huncovce]] (then Hungary, now Slovakia) in the Carpathian Mountains.<ref name="BROWN" /><ref name="LEIMAN" /> He was appointed ''[[Beth din|dayyan]]'' (judge) and also worked as a merchant.<ref name="Patai" /> According to Meir Gilon in ''R. David Friesenhausen: Between the Poles of Haskalah and Hasidut'', Friesenhausen moved from Berlin to its polar opposite Huncovce because he grew disenchanted with the haskala movement in Berlin who in general rejected the divine authorship of the Torah and belief in God.<ref name="BROWN" /><ref name="LEIMAN" />  Friesenhausen married again in [[Huncovce]].<ref name="LEIMAN" />

In 1806, having become unhappy with the isolation of [[Huncovce]], Friesenhausen moved to [[Pest, Hungary|Pest]].<ref name="Patai" /> In Pest, Friesenhausen began to advocate for government oversighted rabbinical seminaries  in Hungary, Galicia, and the Czech lands.<ref name="YIVO" /><ref name="Patai" /> Under Friesenhausen's proposal only graduates of these seminaries would be appointed to the rabbinate.<ref name="YIVO" /> The seminaries would mandate a curriculum of primarily Talmud, but also of Bible, humanities, and sciences, and gym.<ref name="YIVO" />  Friesenhausen was the first to make such a proposal and submitted  his plan to the [[Archduke Joseph, Palatine of Hungary]].<ref name="JE1906">{{cite book|title=The Jewish Encyclopedia: FRIESENHAUSEN, DAVID BEN MEÏR|url=https://jewishencyclopedia.com/articles/6395-friesenhausen-david-ben-meir|year=1906|publisher= [[Funk & Wagnalls]]}}</ref> On 26 July 1806 Friesenhausen met with Archduke Joseph, who promised to bring the matter to his brother [[Francis II, Holy Roman Emperor]].<ref name="Patai" /> The Hungarian rabbinate were unhappy with Friesenhausen's unilateral activities.<ref name="Patai" /> They accused of him being a dangerous reformer and of undermining their position.<ref name="Patai" />  Friesenhausen was unable to attain a rabbinic position in Pest so he moved back to Huncovce.<ref name="Patai" />

In 1813, after some deliberation, the government declined the proposal.<ref name="YIVO" /> The stated reasons were that: (1) The Jews did not have enough funds for the schools especially since the [[tolerance tax]] was increased; (2) the policy of the government was to assimilate the Jews; and (3) Jews were able to attend Christian schools.<ref name="Patai" />

== Sátoraljaújhely ==
Friesenhausen had difficulties making a reasonable income in Huncovce.<ref name="BROWN" /> In 1808, Friesenhausen moved to [[Sátoraljaújhely]] (Ujhely), Hungary, where he served as ''dayyan'' in the rabbinic court of [[Moshe Teitelbaum (Ujhel)|Moses Teitelbaum]].<ref name="BROWN" /> Friesenhausen was unhappy in Sátoraljaújhely, mainly due to his dislike of Moses Teitelbaum.<ref name="BROWN" />

Friesenhausen wrote  ''Mosedot Tebel'', a treatise on astronomy, in which he explains the [[Copernican heliocentrism]].<ref name="LEIMAN" />  ''Mosedot Tebel'' also contains a proof for the eleventh axiom of [[Euclid]], and a 74-page ethical Will & Testament to his children.<ref name="YIVO" /><ref name="LEIMAN" />  In 1816, Friesenhausen left Sátoraljaújhely in order to secure financing for the publication of his book, eventually getting it published in Vienna in 1820.<ref name="LEIMAN" />

== Later life ==
After publishing ''Mosedot Tebel'', Friesenhausen retired and spent his remaining years in [[Alba Iulia]] with his son Meir, a physician.<ref name="YIVO" /><ref name="LEIMAN" /> David died on 23 March 1828.<ref name="YIVO" />

== Further reading ==
